newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee trade expects no changes from ACPC.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee trade expects no changes from ACPC.

text.p: A meeting of the technical committee of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to be held on March 20 in London is not expected to make any changes to quota agreements, traders said.
"I don't think anything will happen...Nothing will change, nothing should change," said Jair Coser, president of leading exporter Unicafe.
The meeting has been called to review the market situation and prepare recommendations for the next full ACPC council, expected to be held in May.

Indonesia's representative to the ACPC Paian Nainggolan has said the meeting is expected to review a decision taken in Rio de Janeiro in January to cut a further 1.3 million 60-kg bags of coffee from exports in the first six months of this year.
But the Ivory Coast's Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze has subsequently said additional cuts will still be implemented.
Of the 300,000 bags of arabica coffee included in the cut, Brazil is to contribute 140,000 bags, giving an export limit for the January to June semester of 5.86 million bags.
Traders said they understood the meeting had been called at the request of Central American nations which were perhaps seeking to increase the supply of arabica coffee to the market.
But in the case of Brazil, there is a growing feeling that the country will not be able to export any more than its current quota given domestic availability.
Exports in the first two months of this year were 2.33 million bags and expectations for March are of 1.2 million bags.
As of March 10, some 240,408 bags had exported this month based on bills of lading while certificates of origin had been issued against 385,577 bags.
April shipments are forecast to be similar to March but it is May and June that exports are now seen to fall off sharply.
One of the main problems which the ACPC meeting is expected to address is the discount at which robusta coffee is trading to arabica, traders said.
"I've never seen anything like it. It's almost like two different commodities, like coffee and tea," one trader said.
"But what is the solution - either you increase the supply of arabica coffee or you take more robusta coffee out of the market? It's a tough one," he added.

Brazil's top commodities official has already said that Brazil will discuss the situation at the ACPC meeting and not before. For the time being there are no meetings planned between government and private sector officials on the issue.

Private sector representatives are next scheduled to meet on March 19 to discuss the problems facing the domestic soluble industry but this may be cancelled in the light of the ACPC talks, officials said.
